COMP7507 · GROUP 3 · FINAL REPORT PART I / OBJECTIVES & HIGHLIGHTS

Objectives, highlights, and architecture

From a visible leaderboard shift to a five-chapter, multi-source exploratory visual analytics platform.

Project Objectives

Between May 2023 and September 2026, the top of the LM Arena text leaderboard shifted from open-weight university and community releases to a proprietary Top 10 controlled by three companies. This project builds an explorable, five-chapter visual analytics report with three concrete objectives: (1) to trace how leaderboard composition, weight-access tiers, and the open-vs-closed frontier rank gap evolved across 41 monthly snapshots; (2) to contextualize that shift beside heterogeneous evidence on organizational financial scale, mapped academic output, estimated training costs, compute ceilings, recorded evaluation attention, open-model supply, talent netflow, and U.S. business AI adoption; and (3) to enforce strict visual-analytics discipline by keeping non-equivalent units separated, preserving missingness, and distinguishing observed association from unproven causation.

Highlights of Work (Three Key Contributions)

1. A nuanced empirical discovery — “Closed Frontier, Open Commons.” Visual exploration refuted a simplistic one-way extinction of open models: while all 10 leading models in the final September 2026 Arena snapshot were closed-weight (7 Anthropic, 2 Google, 1 Meta), open-weight models still held 9 of the Top 50 ranks (18%), DeepSeek R1 briefly took #1 in Jan–Feb 2025, and quarterly new Hugging Face model repositories nearly tripled from 118,252 (2024Q1) to 332,098 (2025Q4) [1, 2, 6].
2. A unified, state-preserving exploratory visual analytics platform. We delivered a locally runnable Python/HTML editorial report integrating five chapter-specific interactive dashboards (D3/Canvas + ECharts) under a shared design grammar, persistent iframe shell, cross-filtering, brush-and-link controls, and keyboard-accessible help dialogs—verified across 77 chart instances and 30 responsive screenshots.
3. Epistemic rigor built directly into visual encodings. Rather than forcing incompatible sources into a single composite index or dual-axis “scissors gap,” every view preserves source-specific denominators, marks incomplete years (dashed 2025 publications) and underfilled pools (pre-Feb 2024 Arena), displays survey uncertainty bands (±1.645 SE), and supports robustness checks (Top 10 vs. Top 50; Fixed-61 models).

Four Reproducible Visual-Analytics Rules

Rule 1 · Overall-only core rankings. Chapters 1, 4, and 5 compute primary leaderboard statistics strictly from Arena's overall category, avoiding double-counting across overlapping subcategories (which remain interactive filter options in Ch1).
Rule 2 · Keep missingness visible. Underfilled pre-Feb 2024 pools are never labeled a full Top 50; missing snapshot months use hatched gaps; incomplete 2025 publications render dashed; unknown licenses remain a distinct category.
Rule 3 · Never mix incompatible units. Market capitalization, audited 10-K revenue, annualized run rates, recorded evaluation shares, and HF repository counts occupy separate panels and scales—never subtracted or merged into one index.
Rule 4 · Triangulation, not causal proof. Parallel timing across seven source families illuminates plausible economic barriers (e.g., training costs vs. academic share) without claiming measured user movement or causal identification.

Chapter 1 — The Flip: Leaderboard shift

Open-weight share contracted sharply at the top, yet remained active in the Top 50 and briefly reclaimed #1 in early 2025.

Figure 1. Left (A): Open-weight share of the Arena overall Top 50 across full-pool months (Feb 2024–Sep 2026), falling from 40/50 (80%) to 9/50 (18%). Right (B): Signed frontier rank gap (best open-weight rank minus best closed-weight rank, Dec 2023–Sep 2026). Positive values indicate closed-weight leadership; negative values mark open-weight leadership (DeepSeek R1 at rank #1 in Jan–Feb 2025). Rank difference is ordinal, not a linear capability score [1].

Key Empirical Findings

  • Complete proprietary concentration at the Top 10, not an empty open commons. By the final local Arena snapshot (11 Sep 2026; 401 models in pool), every Top-10 position was held by closed-weight proprietary models from just three organizations: Anthropic (7 models, led by claude-fable-5.1-max), Google (2 models), and Meta (1 model, muse-spark-1.2). Yet 9 open-weight models remained inside the Top 50 (18%, or 16% under strict Apache/MIT licenses), positioned at ranks 17, 22, 23, 28, 31, 32, 36, 42, and 50 [1].
  • Non-monotonic trajectory and the DeepSeek R1 counter-example. Rather than a smooth monotonic collapse, the open-weight Top-50 share rebounded several times during 2025. More strikingly, the signed frontier rank gap widened from +2 ranks in Dec 2023 to +10 in Oct 2024, inverted to −1 in January and February 2025 when open-weight DeepSeek R1 held #1 overall, and then widened again to +16 ranks by September 2026 (best open-weight model at rank #17).
  • Cutoff and license-definition sensitivity. Comparing Top 10 against Top 50—and toggling Apache/MIT permissive licenses versus restricted community licenses (e.g., Llama, Gemma, Qwen)—demonstrates that headline claims about “open-source collapse” depend heavily on both the rank cutoff and the legal definition of openness.

Why Two Complementary Narrative Views Matter

Showing only an endpoint bar chart (May 2023 vs. September 2026) exaggerates the shift by hiding early pool incompleteness (only 10–46 models before Feb 2024) and erasing mid-period open-weight surges. Pairing the continuous Top-50 share curve (Figure 1A) with the signed frontier gap anchored at a zero baseline (Figure 1B) directly addresses both pitfalls, while deferring model-level inspection to the interactive Chapter 1 dashboard (Figure 2).

Chapter 1 — Interactive D3/Canvas dashboard

From aggregate percentages to model-by-model rank inspection across 29 Arena categories and 41 monthly snapshots.

Figure 2. Delivered Chapter 1 interactive dashboard (/explore/ch1/), built with D3 scales/shapes on HTML5 Canvas paired with an SVG interactive monthly ruler. Each tile encodes one model in rank order (green = open-weight, terracotta = closed-weight, gray outline = tied ranks); the vertical dashed line at 2023.12 marks the end of incomplete early closed-weight coverage.

Visual Encoding & Interaction Design Rationale

Visual Cues & Marks

  • Rank-preserving discrete blocks: Unlike smoothed area charts that hide individual releases and tied ranks, the default matrix renders one tile per model-month, keeping ties visible with subtle gray borders and leaving underfilled pre-2024 seats blank rather than rescaled.
  • Color & license granularity: Muted forest green (open-weight) and terracotta red (closed-weight) maintain high contrast within the report palette; toggling Apache / MIT detail splits open weights into dark vs. light green without altering totals.
  • Explicit missingness encoding: Hatched gray bands distinguish months lacking snapshots from zero values; the pre-Dec 2023 region explicitly warns of incomplete closed-model coverage.

Explorative Interactions

  • Multi-mode morphing transitions: Switching between Original rank, Area composition (overall or 3-tier: 1–10 / 11–30 / 31–50), and Frontier gap animates each model tile continuously across views (1450 ms D3 interpolation, respecting reduced-motion settings).
  • 29 Arena categories & Top-10/Top-50 scope: Users test whether the flip holds in coding, math, hard prompts, or non-English leaderboards via the Category selector (mirrored in deep-link URLs such as ?category=coding).
  • Linked month inspection: Hovering previews any month's shares on the SVG ruler; clicking locks the month and updates the bottom KPI strip and full model-level license table.

Chapter 2 — Divergence: Scale and output

Public market value and private-lab revenue paces rose sharply while mapped corporate AI publication counts fell.

Figure 3. Delivered Chapter 2 interactive dashboard (/explore/ch2/). Four coordinated ECharts cards separate incompatible organizational metrics: (2.1) listed-company market cap, audited SEC 10-K annual revenue, and within-cohort share stacks; (2.2) private AI-lab annualized revenue run rates (linear/log toggle); (2.3) max-year revenue scale; and (2.4) ETO mapped AI publications (solid 2023–24, dashed incomplete 2025) [2, 5, 7].

Key Empirical Findings: Economic Growth vs. Academic Output

  • Rapid expansion across both public giants and private labs. From Jan 2023 to Sep 2026, all five tracked public companies grew substantially in market cap: NVIDIA surged 11.0× ($479B → $5.27T), Meta 4.3× ($387B → $1.65T), Alphabet 3.2× ($1.28T → $4.14T), Amazon 2.6× ($1.05T → $2.77T), and Microsoft 2.1× ($1.79T → $3.68T). Audited annual revenues rose in parallel (NVIDIA 8.0×, from $27.0B in FY23 to $215.9B in FY26; Amazon $574.8B → $716.9B) [5].
  • Steep private-lab revenue run-rate trajectories. Reported annualized run rates climbed from $0.2B (Mar 2023) to $25.0B (Feb 2026) at OpenAI and from $0.1B (Oct 2023) to $19.0B (Mar 2026) at Anthropic, while xAI ($0.43B), Mistral AI ($0.40B), and Z.ai ($0.05B) remained orders of magnitude smaller [2].
  • Declining recorded corporate AI publications. Even strictly within complete ETO years (2023 → 2024), mapped AI publications fell across major corporate research labs: Alphabet/Google dropped 33.9% (951 → 629), Alibaba/Qwen 37.7% (727 → 453), Meta 25.7% (439 → 326), and OpenAI 40.9% (22 → 13). Incomplete 2025 figures (rendered dashed) continue downward [7].
  • Visual design & interaction rationale. We deliberately rejected a composite “organizational strength score” and never assigned fictitious market caps to private labs. Interactive Compare group, Organization, and Year range filters allow users to isolate cohorts while the Keep unselected data (greyed out) toggle preserves full-cohort context and keeps stacked share denominators fixed.

Chapter 3 — The Cost Cliff & academic exit

Estimated frontier training costs reached hundreds of millions of dollars alongside a sharp contraction in academia's notable-model share.

Figure 4. Delivered Chapter 3 interactive dashboard (/explore/ch3/). Top: (3.1) Log-scale Epoch training cost scatter (n=288 models ≥$0.8M, 2023–26; FLOP-proxy filled, Open/Closed filter, ~1.83×/yr trendline); (3.2) Lollipop benchmark of institutional capital divided by a single $366M GPT-4.5 training run. Bottom: (3.3a) AI Index notable model origin shares; (3.3b) Compute gap (FLOPs, academic ceiling ≈1024); (3.3c) Frontier lab annual spending ($B) [2, 3, 10].

Key Empirical Findings & Design Rationale

  • Multi-order-of-magnitude training cost escalation. Across the 288 models ≥$0.8M in the 2023–2026 display window (254 Industry, 34 Academia), estimated training costs span three orders of magnitude (~1.83×/yr mean trend across this subset; ~2.4×/yr among frontier models), reaching $218M (Grok 3), $264M (GPT-5), $366M (GPT-4.5), and $388M (Grok 4) [3].
  • Order-of-magnitude funding threshold. Benchmarked against a $366M GPT-4.5 run (1.0× dashed line), illustrative academic budgets cover 0.005× ($2M lab) to 0.041× ($15M top university HPC), and independent startups like AI21 (0.82×) and Runway (0.86×) fall below 1.0×. Meanwhile, Anthropic and OpenAI annual spending jumped from $2.5B→$7.0B and $4.0B→$16.0B (2024→2025) [2, 10].
  • Collapse of independent academic notable models. In Stanford AI Index data, academia's standalone share of notable AI models dropped from 15.1% (2023) to 3.1% (2024) and 1.1% (2025), while industry rose from 58.0% to 91.6% and academic compute clustered near a ~1024 FLOP ceiling versus 1025–1026+ FLOPs in industry [2].
  • Visual design & epistemic bounds. Logarithmic y/x-axes make 1000× cost and funding spans readable; red/blue sector hues pair with diamond (open) vs. circle (closed) shapes, and the Open/Closed filter plus Reset all chart views button let users verify that high costs occur across both access types. Crucially, the 1.0× line is framed as an order-of-magnitude benchmark—not an audited solvency test or sole causal proof.

Chapter 4 — Parallel trends in the ecosystem

Proprietary evaluation share and open-platform repository supply expanded simultaneously alongside slowing talent netflow and rising U.S. adoption.

Figure 5. Delivered Chapter 4 interactive dashboard (/explore/ch4/) in the default 2024–25 window, integrating four top KPI cards, a global date brush, scoped panel filters (Models, Country, Fixed 61, Full weeks, 90% interval, Events), and four aligned ecosystem views [1, 2, 4, 6].
Figure 6. Full-window (All dates) summary of Chapter 4's four non-equivalent tracks: (A) Proprietary evaluation share rising 50.28%→56.17% (2024Q1–25Q4) and 60.37% (2026Q3), with Fixed-61 robustness check (50.74%→64.23%); (B) HF quarterly new repositories (118.3k→332.1k; 1.93M total); (C) U.S. talent netflow (320.4→26.0, −91.9% yet still positive); (D) U.S. BTOS Q7 adoption (3.7%→10.0% with 90% CI) [1, 2, 4, 6].

Findings & Semantically Scoped Interaction Design

Chapter 4 refutes a simplistic “closed replaces open” story: proprietary recorded evaluation share and Hugging Face repository additions both rose across 2024–2025 (with quarterly fluctuations), while the 15-week Arena 140k battle sample (135,624 valid battles, 53 models, 11.62% both-bad) shows rapid turnover in weekly model exposure (default Top 5 peaking at 28.03% in Jun 2025). By keeping global date brushing separate from panel-specific controls—so selecting a country only updates Talent Netflow and selecting models only updates Exposure—the dashboard prevents invalid cross-denominator comparisons while letting users click any date to align cross-panel timing.

How interactive visual analytics challenged initial hypotheses, exposed denominator traps, and shaped our final conclusions.

Effectiveness Criteria Achieved Across the Workflow

Overview first, zoom & filter, details on demand (Shneiderman's Mantra). Readers begin with concise editorial Storyboard figures (2 summary charts per chapter), expand any chapter panel inline or full screen without losing scroll or filter state, and hover/click into individual models, companies, or survey windows.
Built-in sensitivity & robustness testing. Rather than asking readers to trust a single aggregation choice, the dashboards expose live robustness toggles: Top 10 vs. Top 50 and Apache/MIT detail (Ch1), greyed-out cohort context (Ch2), Open vs. Closed cost filtering (Ch3), Fixed-61 & Full-weeks toggles (Ch4), and Log vs. Linear rank scale (Ch5).

Methods, architecture, and design trade-offs

How we evolved from our initial Tableau proposal to a verified, state-preserving Python/HTML visual analytics platform.

Implemented System Architecture

The final work product is a self-contained web application served locally by Python Flask + Waitress (app.py mounting Ch2 and Ch3 via Werkzeug DispatcherMiddleware, plus static/API routes for Storyboard, Ch1, Ch4, and Ch5). All visualization libraries, local InterVariable fonts, and frozen extracts ship inside work_package/—requiring zero external CDNs or raw archives. Shared tokens (chart-theme.css, chart-theme.js, embed.css) unify ECharts (Storyboard, Ch2–Ch5) and D3/Canvas + SVG (Ch1). During Ruan Lixin's architecture refactor (PR #1), a custom embed-bridge.js protocol kept every chapter iframe alive in place across collapse, expansion, and fullscreen so users retain zoom, brush, and filter state.

Methods Tried, Retired, and Justified

Design DimensionAlternative Considered / TriedFinal Implemented ChoiceAnalytical & Engineering Justification
Platform & StackTableau single-wide-table workbook (COMP7507_Ch5.twbx)Python Flask + HTML/JS (ECharts + D3/Canvas) with persistent iframesHeterogeneous source grains (daily, biweekly, monthly, quarterly, irregular) broke single-table joins; web stack enables custom Canvas rank blocks, responsive layouts, and zero-license local execution.
Ch1 Rendering EngineStatic Matplotlib / Recharts SVG chartsD3 scales/shapes on HTML5 Canvas + SVG monthly rulerRendering 50×41 = 2,050 animated model blocks smoothly with 1450 ms morphing transitions across 29 categories required Canvas performance while preserving crisp SVG hover rulers.

Difficulties and unimplemented plans

What proved hardest across heterogeneous datasets and multi-member engineering—and what we intentionally left undone.

Key Difficulties Encountered & How We Resolved Them

  • Cross-source schema drift and entity alignment: Organization strings varied widely across 10 raw datasets (e.g., Alphabet (including Google) in ETO, comma-delimited multi-org strings in Epoch AI, and 61 drifting model-to-organization mappings in LM Arena). We constructed explicit crosswalk rules, separated unmapped entities rather than imputing zeros, and verified every chapter against frozen JSON/CSV extracts.
  • Unifying five independently built dashboards into one coherent user experience: Each member initially authored their chapter using different libraries and visual styles (React/Vite in Ch1, Dash/Plotly in Ch2, Flask/Plotly in Ch3, standalone HTML/JS in Ch4, ECharts in Ch5). Unifying colors, typography, help dialogs, and fullscreen/return navigation without breaking chapter-specific logic required an extensive architectural refactor (PR #1) followed by iterative member PRs (#2–#9) and automated baseline-hash verification.
  • Handling irregular time windows and incomplete late-period records: Source windows ended on different dates (Arena Sep 2026; BTOS & Talent Sep 2025; HF supply Dec 2025; ETO 2025 incomplete; SEC FY2026 partial). Keeping missing periods blank, adding dashed incomplete segments, and introducing Ch4's preset window buttons (2024–25, Battle window, All dates) prevented misleading endpoint comparisons.
  • Preventing over-claiming during narrative editing: Early drafts used strong causal language (“cost forced academia out,” “users migrated to proprietary models”). Iterative critique across demo rehearsal and code reviews forced us to trim claims strictly to what each dataset actually observes.

COMP7507 · GROUP 3 · FINAL REPORT PART I / LIMITATIONS & FUTURE WORK

Limitations of data, visuals, and tools

Explicit boundaries on measurement validity, visual encodings, software engineering trade-offs, and directions for future research.

Data & Measurement Limitations

Leaderboard & Evaluation Limits (Ch1, Ch4):
  • LM Arena pools evolve dynamically; scoring and sampling policies shifted on 2024-01-09, 2025-05-16 (default style control), and 2025-07-23.
  • Rank differences are ordinal, not cardinal capability margins; “open-weight” does not guarantee OSI-compliant open-source training data or commercial rights.
  • 22.4% of adjacent leaderboard vote-count deltas are negative; recorded votes reflect platform sampling, not real-world market share.
Economic, Cost & Ecosystem Limits (Ch2, Ch3, Ch4):
  • Epoch training costs combine estimates and FLOP-based proxies ($4×10−18/FLOP when direct cost is missing) and omit post-training, data, and inference spending.
  • The $366M GPT-4.5 run is a single illustrative benchmark; total venture funding is not liquid capital allocable to one pre-training run.
  • New HF repositories measure upload volume (including fine-tunes and adapters), not frontier capability or active usage; BTOS measures broad U.S. AI use only.

Visualization & Tooling Limitations

  • Canvas rendering vs. accessibility and vector export (Ch1): Rendering Ch1's 2,050 rank blocks on HTML5 Canvas delivers smooth 60 fps D3 morphing animations, but Canvas pixels cannot be natively searched, screen-read, or exported as vector paths; we mitigated this by pairing Canvas with an accessible SVG hover ruler and an HTML monthly detail table.
  • Logarithmic scale constraints (Ch3, Ch5): Log axes are essential to display $0.8M–$400M+ training costs and 0.005×–20.5× funding ratios legibly, but log scales exclude zero or negative observations and can visually compress large absolute dollar differences at the top end (mitigated in Ch2/Ch5 via explicit Linear/Log toggles).
  • Iframe architecture and local server dependency: Embedding five independent dashboards via persistent iframes preserved member autonomy and interactive state, but introduces cross-frame height/scroll synchronization complexity (handled by embed-bridge.js) and requires running a local Python Flask server (bash start.sh) rather than opening a single serverless HTML file.
  • Static local snapshot ceiling: Because all datasets are frozen through September 2026 for reproducibility, subsequent leaderboard shifts, newly audited FY2026 10-K filings, or revised Epoch cost estimates will not appear automatically.

Prioritized Future Work

To advance this exploratory visual analytics framework toward causal and longitudinal evaluation, future iterations should: (1) freeze machine-readable codebooks and audit every Arena license string model-by-model (distinguishing weights, data, and code openness); (2) incorporate longitudinal enterprise API/cloud telemetry or model-level adoption surveys once available to bridge the firm-to-model gap; (3) propagate explicit cost-estimation confidence intervals onto the Ch3 scatter and funding-multiple views; and (4) package a static WebAssembly/Pyodide or pre-rendered JSON build so the entire five-chapter platform can be hosted on GitHub Pages without a Python backend.

Details of Tasks Completed

  • Early Proposal Stage (B, C): Participated in early multi-source dataset inspection, feasibility verification, and proposal drafting; designed the Chapter 2 separation between listed-company financial tracks and private-lab observations.
  • Chapter 2 Data Pipeline & Interactive Dashboard: Built the Chapter 2 Flask/ECharts module (dashboards/ch2/), assembling 45 monthly market-capitalization observations for five listed AI leaders (close × historical shares outstanding via yfinance), extracting audited annual 10-K revenues from SEC EDGAR company-facts JSONs (350–380 day windows), integrating Stanford AI Index private-lab annualized revenue run rates (fig_4.2.18), and mapping ETO yearly AI publication records.
  • Interactive Controls, Visual Polish & Testing (PRs #3, #6): Implemented coordinated Compare group, Organizations, and Year range filters, Linear/Log y-axis toggling for lab run rates, a Keep unselected data (greyed out) toggle preserving fixed cohort denominators, click-to-filter cross-chart selection, layout refinements, opacity reset fixes, and deterministic state tests (dashboards/ch2/tests/state.test.mjs).

Key Results & Findings

  • Quantified simultaneous economic growth across both cohorts: listed market cap rose 2.1×–11.0× (NVIDIA reaching $5.27T; audited revenue 8.0× to $215.9B in FY26), while reported private-lab run rates climbed to $25.0B (OpenAI) and $19.0B (Anthropic).

Methodological Reflection

Public corporations and private AI labs do not share comparable financial metrics, and late-period coverage (FY2026 10-K filings, 2025 ETO records) is uneven. Resisting the urge to build a single composite score—and instead preserving distinct scales, fixed denominators, and explicit dashed lines for partial years—kept the divergence narrative rigorous and auditable.

  • Chapter 3 Five-Chart Interactive Dashboard: Designed and implemented the Chapter 3 Flask backend and five-panel visualization suite (dashboards/ch3/, static/chapter3-charts.js): (3.1) log-scale training cost scatter combining Epoch costs with FLOP-based proxies ($4×10−18/FLOP) across 288 models ≥$0.8M plus an empirical exponential trendline (~1.83×/yr) and Open/Closed weight filter; (3.2) log-scale lollipop chart comparing institutional funding against a $366M GPT-4.5 training run; (3.3a) AI Index notable-model origin shares; (3.3b) Industry vs. Academia compute gap (FLOPs); and (3.3c) frontier lab annual spending.

Key Results & Findings

  • Showed that estimated frontier pre-training costs escalated to $218M–$388M+, placing typical academic budgets (0.005×–0.041×) and several independent startups (0.82×–0.86×) below a single $366M frontier benchmark run.
  • Linked the cost and compute gap (~1024 FLOP academic ceiling vs. 1025–1026+ FLOP industry runs) with Stanford AI Index evidence showing academia's standalone notable-model share fell from 15.1% (2023) to 1.1% (2025), while Anthropic ($2.5B→$7.0B) and OpenAI ($4.0B→$16.0B) expanded annual spending.

Methodological Reflection

Dividing total institutional funding by an estimated single-run cost compares distinct financial concepts and relies on modeled proxies rather than audited lab budgets. Presenting the 1.0× line explicitly as an order-of-magnitude benchmark—and keeping Open/Closed filtering interactive—communicates the economic barrier without claiming cost was the sole causal driver.

Methodological Reflection

The primary analytical trap in Chapter 4 is conflating four incompatible populations (Arena evaluators, HF uploaders, national LinkedIn talent flows, and U.S. employers). Scoping controls so model selection only affects Exposure and country selection only affects Talent helps keep the interpretation appropriate to each dataset.
